prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language oeuvre of dense, patterned prose, with roots in lyric poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture of rare imaginative scale.

statement.case_for: My preferred laureate is unchanged. The citation scope is narrower than in round 1. Public knowledge of Cărtărescu supports a distinctive voice: hallucinatory, densely patterned Romanian prose in which the body, memory, dream and cosmology form one imaginative system. The longlist names Blinding and Solenoid as representative works. Blinding is presented as the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy. These books appear to be built as cumulative architectures, not as a single stylistic display. That supports a claim about voice, formal and linguistic ambition, and imaginative and intellectual depth across a body of work, which is what the common criteria ask for. I accept the chair questions and the colleagues' points on scope. The citation should name the prose project and its architecture, and treat the poetry as origin and context. It should not claim equal achievement in the poetry, whose translation coverage is thinnest and which I cannot assess. This matches what I can defend, and I would not claim more. The case does not rest on all six members ranking him first, on fame, on age, or on national or political symbolism. Rank agreement is not evidence of merit. I have not read the texts and cannot independently verify any source. These judgments rest on general public knowledge, the shortlist descriptions and my colleagues' accounts.
statement.case_against: The reservations are unchanged and are about evidence, not preference. First, much of the effect is said to lie in Romanian sentence rhythm, density and register, and I can judge it only through translation and secondary description. Second, the maximalist, recursive method may sustain quality across very long books or may restate its motifs. Sward and Sem-Sandberg are right that length alone is not evidence of sustained quality. I cannot settle from the supplied evidence whether the later long works enlarge the project. If expert reading of the Romanian showed that they only restate it, the case would weaken and Adonis would deserve a closer look on formal and linguistic renewal. Third, my evidence does not document Romanian-language expert input. My profile records expert reports only for Asian and African literature. The committee should therefore say plainly that it is judging the prose through translation.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg agrees with the case for Cărtărescu but does not want the major novels to stand in for the whole oeuvre. His citation centres the prose project and treats the poetry as origin and context, since he cannot confirm the poetry has equal weight. He also wants expert reports on the Romanian prose before relying on claims about its sentence-level achievement.
responses.response: I accept this scope and have narrowed my own citation to it. In round 1 I wrote of a Romanian-language oeuvre resting on a poet's attention to the sentence. That phrase risked claiming more for the poetry than my evidence supports. The revised wording places the poetry as roots, not as a co-equal claim. I also agree that size alone cannot count as sustained quality. Where I would add to his point is on what unavailable expert input should do. It should lower the confidence with which the committee states its claim, not change the ranking by itself. The committee should record that the sentence-level judgment is provisional.

responses.point: Palm would keep the citation to the novelistic project so the claim does not rest on the poetry. She holds that recurrence of obsessions is not a weakness in itself and that the question is whether each large work enlarges the project or restates it. She would anchor the citation in the written text and in the formal architecture, not only in the imagery.
responses.response: I agree with her on both scope and the test. The strongest oeuvres return to a few obsessions, so recurrence is not the question. What matters is whether Solenoid, as a later work, develops the architecture of the earlier books or only repeats it. I cannot verify that from the supplied evidence. I would hold her escalation reading as a reasonable hypothesis from public knowledge and not a settled finding. If a member who has read the later volumes closely found only restatement, I would take that as a real reason to move toward Adonis. I would not treat it as a point to be absorbed into the citation wording. I also take her point that the citation should name the architecture, and the revised wording does.

responses.point: Sward holds her preference as provisional. It depends on readers confirming that the later volumes develop the early ones. She also says that Adonis may present a claim as strong in the original Arabic, which she cannot assess without Arabic-language expertise.
responses.response: I agree that the preference is provisional in the way she describes, and my own is provisional in the same way. She also gives the clearest answer to the chair's question about Adonis. I read the difference between Adonis and Cărtărescu as a difference in the evidence available to this committee, not a proven difference in merit. My ranking therefore reflects confidence in the assessment as much as strength of claim. I place Adonis second because renewing the language of a major poetic tradition is a very strong claim. I would move him to equal or first place only if reliable Arabic-language expert accounts of his prosody and his dialogue with inherited forms supported that claim. Age and public commentary would not be reasons to move him.

responses.point: Mattson calls Adonis a very close second and says her preference for Cărtărescu rests on how confidently each case can be assessed across the whole oeuvre, not on a difference in seriousness. She would name the essays only as part of the same project, and she asks how much weight a slim corpus like Michon's can carry for a whole-oeuvre claim.
responses.response: I share that framing and consider it more honest than treating the two cases as unequal in merit. On Adonis, I agree that any citation should keep the verse central and mention the critical writing only as part of the same project. On Michon, I do not know of a stated standard under which a compact oeuvre supports a whole-oeuvre citation, and I do not want to invent one. My view is that concentration is a real form of sustained quality, but the criterion of significance across a body of work needs enough range to show development. The Michon files, mine included, give limited evidence of that. His French syntax is also hard to carry into translation. That is why I keep him fifth in my ordering and outside my alternatives. It is not a judgment against his achievement.

responses.point: Carlberg's citation names a prose and poetic oeuvre. She keeps Adonis as her first alternative and says Arabic-language expert assessment is unavailable. Her round 1 response to me also describes my ranking as including Kincaid.
responses.response: I would narrow her citation to the prose, for the reason above: the poetry's translation coverage is thinnest, and I cannot confirm it carries equal weight. On her description of my ranking, I should correct the record. My opening ranking did not include Kincaid, and Kincaid is not on this shortlist. Mine ran Cărtărescu, Adonis, Zurita, Michon, Can Xue, Murnane and Robinson in that order. I agree with the substance of her main point. Adonis is the strongest alternative, and the open question is verification and not an argument against the poems.

uncertainties: How much of the Romanian sentence rhythm, density and register survives in translation, including Swedish editions, cannot be judged from the supplied evidence, and no Romanian-language expert input is documented in my record.

Whether the later long works, including Solenoid, deepen the architecture of the Orbitor trilogy or restate its motifs remains unsettled. Specific passages or volumes cannot be named on the supplied evidence.
Whether the poetry and early fiction sustain the level of the major novels is unestablished. This is why the citation treats the poetry as origin and context.
Whether the difference between Adonis and Cărtărescu lies in merit or only in the committee's evidence cannot be resolved without Arabic-language expert accounts.
Whether Zurita's non-textual works can be assessed as literature is open. Any citation for him should rest on the page-based sequences.
I have not read any of the works. All judgments rest on general public knowledge, the shortlist descriptions and colleagues' accounts.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile. My scholarly work on Celan, the fragment, exile literature, modern poetry and Ekelöf is context and not evidence of preference for any candidate, and the profile records no personal or professional tie to a shortlisted writer. My ceremony speeches were given on behalf of the Academy and do not establish a personal preference. I have not recused myself and none is asserted. Disclosed conflicts for other members are noted but not adjudicated. Some round 1 responses referred to writers who are not on this shortlist, such as Kincaid and Wright. I set those references aside.
